title: Fix install upgrade path and republish a working launcher

history.detail:
FAIL: FAIL — Round 1. Audited commit 10b2f0a against the current sprint 2 file, re-read fresh. Working tree clean apart from the known out-of-scope .vscode/settings.json.

What's right: the taxonomy is explicit data, not scattered conditionals (Req 1). .claude/agents and CLAUDE.md are correctly user-owned — I verified by hand that a customised persona survives an upgrade untouched, which is the misclassification the sprint's Risks section says would be most destructive. package.json is 0.1.1 and tag v0.1.1 points at 10b2f0a, i.e. at the code that would actually publish rather than at the earlier bump commit (Req 6). scripts/verify-tarball.sh is a real, runnable procedure and I ran it end-to-end: it passes, and I independently confirmed via npm pack that the tarball now carries only the .gitkeep skeleton (Req 7). scripts/launcher/** is byte-identical to sprint 1's closed state, satisfying the regression criterion. 54 tests pass, run by me.

Three defects. Two are in code this sprint wrote.

BLOCKER 1 — backups are re-consumed as stale framework files on every subsequent run, and the chain grows without bound. A backup written by overwriteFrameworkFile()/removeStaleFrameworkFile() lands *inside* a FRAMEWORK_OWNED directory (e.g. scripts/launcher/run-role.js.bak-0.1.0). On the next run, syncFrameworkPath() collects it in destFilesBefore, doesn't find it in sourceSet, and routes it to removeStaleFrameworkFile(). Reproduced with three real upgrade runs against a simulated stale install:
  run 1 -> run-role.js.bak-0.1.0, state.js.bak-0.1.0
  run 2 -> run-role.js.bak-0.1.0.bak-0.1.1, state.js.bak-0.1.0.bak-0.1.1
  run 3 -> run-role.js.bak-0.1.0.bak-0.1.1.bak-0.1.1
Consequences, in order of how much they matter:
  - Req 2 says overwriting must always be recoverable. After three runs the user's original run-role.js is at run-role.js.bak-0.1.0.bak-0.1.1.bak-0.1.1. That is recoverable only in the sense that the bytes still exist somewhere; nobody will find it.
  - Idempotency is gone. install.js's own summary invites a re-run ("re-run this script if useful"), and a plain re-run with nothing to upgrade now mutates the tree every time. The existing "re-running against its own output is a no-op" test does not catch this because a first install creates no backups — the test and the bug don't intersect.
  - The Removed section reports the installer's own backups as "no longer part of the framework", which is a false statement printed to the user about files the installer itself just wrote.
  - Filenames grow by ~11 bytes per run. Somewhere around 20-25 upgrades this exceeds the 255-byte filename limit and copyFileSync throws ENAMETOOLONG, so the installer eventually fails outright rather than degrading.
Note that LiveQA's Part A upgrade check runs the installer once and would pass. This only appears on the second run.

BLOCKER 2 — a local install copies this repo's live sprint data into the target project. docs/sprints is classified USER_OWNED, which means "copy from source when absent". Running `node /path/to/fully-completely/scripts/install.js` from an empty project — the invocation install.js's own header documents — produced, in my throwaway target:
  docs/sprints/registry.json (this repo's, listing sprints 1 and 2, next_id 3)
  docs/sprints/state/sprint-1.json and sprint-2.json (containing my full QA1 audit text and the maintainer's email address)
  docs/sprints/3-done/sprint-1_...md and 2-in-progress/sprint-2_...md
  docs/sprints/.locks/*.lock (transient lock files, gitignored, copied anyway because collectPaths walks the real filesystem)
This is not only an information leak. The target project now starts life with a registry claiming two sprints exist that have nothing to do with it, so /sprint-new hands out 3 and /sprint-status 1 reports another project's history — the target's sprint state is corrupt from the first command.

To be fair about provenance: docs/sprints was already in the old COPY_PATHS, so the behaviour predates this sprint and is not a regression introduced here. But Req 1 is precisely "classify every installed path", this sprint is the one that made the call, and the comment written above USER_OWNED asserts that "this repo's copy of docs/sprints/ only ever supplies the initial empty-folder skeleton on a genuine first install". That is false for the local-install path, and a comment that states a safety property the code doesn't have is worse than no comment. The .npmignore fix is correct and I confirmed it works, but it fixes the packaging layer while the classification defect it compensates for stays in place — so exactly one of the two documented install paths is safe. USER_OWNED is the wrong category: the correct behaviour is to seed only the phase-folder skeleton and never copy source sprint content at all, in either path.

Answering the direct question on scoping: yes, treating the tarball leak as part of Req 7 was the right call — Req 7 is "verify the tarball before publishing", and discovering the tarball is wrong is the entire point of verifying it. Escalating would have been process for its own sake. The judgement was right; the fix was just applied one layer too far downstream.

FINDING 3 — a symlinked directory inside a framework-owned tree routes deletion outside the framework-owned set. Req 4's acceptance criterion asks me to confirm no input can do this, so I tested it rather than reading it. collectPaths() uses fs.statSync, which follows symlinks, so a symlink at scripts/launcher/linked pointing to ../../my-precious is walked into, and its contents are collected as scripts/launcher/linked/* and treated as stale. Result, reproduced:
  scripts/launcher/linked/notes.txt (no longer part of the framework, backed up ..., then removed)
and the user's my-precious/notes.txt — plainly outside the framework-owned set — was deleted, leaving only notes.txt.bak-0.1.0 in their own directory. Content survives via the backup, so this is not silent data loss, but Req 4 says "Never delete anything outside the framework-owned set" without qualification, and this is a route to exactly that. The fix is small: use fs.lstatSync in collectPaths and refuse to descend into or collect symlinks. Contrived setup, real violation, cheap fix — I'd rather it be closed than argued about.

MINOR — removeDeadGitignoreLines() rewrites the whole .gitignore as raw.split(/\r?\n/).join('\n'), silently converting a CRLF file to LF whenever a dead line is found. Harmless on macOS, but Part B is Windows and this sprint's whole point is that Windows is where the unverified things break. Preserve the file's existing line ending.

On the classification question for the paths the sprint file didn't name: I agree with all of them. scripts/smoke_test.sh, dev2_worktree.sh, worktree_test.sh, install.js and docs/HUMAN_OVERRIDE.md are shipped and maintained upstream and are not customisation surfaces, which is the actual test — "does the user edit this on purpose", not "does it look like a framework file". install.js overwriting itself mid-run is safe: Node reads the module fully at require time, so the running process is unaffected by the replacement. docs/sprints is the only one you got wrong, and it's wrong in the other direction — see Blocker 2.

Required before re-audit: stop treating installer-written backups as framework files (exclude the backup naming pattern from the stale scan, or keep backups outside the framework tree entirely); make docs/sprints seed the skeleton only, in both install paths, and correct the comment; make collectPaths symlink-safe; preserve .gitignore line endings. Add tests for the second-run case specifically — the current no-op test cannot see it — and for the symlink case. Then re-run /sprint-qa1 2.

Nothing here touches Req 6's publish step, which is Pipeman's and which I do not gate on. But this must not publish in its current state: publishing is irreversible, the audience includes workshop students, and a first upgrade cycle would hand them a corrupted registry.

PASS: PASS — Round 2. Audited commit 5628f95 against the current sprint 2 file, re-read fresh and confirmed unchanged since round 1 (last touched at 10b2f0a, no working-tree diff). Working tree otherwise clean apart from the known out-of-scope .vscode/settings.json.

All three blockers and the minor finding are fixed. I re-ran my own round-1 reproductions against the new code rather than accepting the handoff's account of them — which mattered here, because the handoff text arrived corrupted partway through (the test count, the git-tag note, and the closing line were garbled). None of the conclusions below come from that text.

BLOCKER 1 (backup compounding) — FIXED. Backups now carry a distinct .fc-bak- marker and collectPaths() filters any path whose basename contains it, so a backup is never re-collected as stale framework content. Re-ran my exact three-run repro against a simulated stale install:
  run 1: Upgraded 0.1.0 -> 0.1.1, backups run-role.js.fc-bak-0.1.0 and state.js.fc-bak-0.1.0
  run 2: Already at 0.1.1 (re-run, nothing to upgrade), same two backups, no Removed section
  run 3: identical
No nesting, no unbounded filename growth, no false "no longer part of the framework" reports, and idempotency is restored — runs 2 and 3 are genuine no-ops. Req 2's recoverability now means something in practice: the original run-role.js sits at exactly one obvious name, one hop from where it was, and I read its contents back to confirm.

BLOCKER 2 (sprint-data leak) — FIXED, and fixed at the right layer this time. docs/sprints is no longer walked; SPRINT_SKELETON_FILES is an explicit seven-entry allowlist of phase-folder .gitkeep placeholders, special-cased in the USER_OWNED loop. A real local install into an empty directory now produces exactly those seven files and nothing else — no registry.json, zero state/*.json, no sprint markdown, and no .locks/*.lock (which the old directory walk was picking up as a side effect of reading the real filesystem). Confirmed by find over a fresh throwaway target and by grepping it for audit text and the maintainer's email: absent. Both documented install paths are now safe, rather than the packaging layer alone. The comment above USER_OWNED has been rewritten to describe what the code actually enforces and to record why, which is the right correction — the previous version asserted a safety property the code did not have.

BLOCKER 3 (symlink escape) — FIXED. collectPaths() uses lstatSync and returns [] for a symlink rather than descending. Re-ran my exact scenario — a symlinked directory under scripts/launcher/ pointing at an external directory holding a user file — and the external file survives untouched, with no Removed section emitted at all. Req 4's "never delete anything outside the framework-owned set" now holds against the one input I found that could route around it.

MINOR (CRLF) — FIXED for the path Req 4 covers. removeDeadGitignoreLines() detects the file's existing ending and rejoins with it. Verified on a real CRLF .gitignore: the dead line is removed and the surviving lines keep their CRLF endings.

Regression checks, all re-run rather than assumed:
- scripts/launcher/** is byte-identical to sprint 1's closed state across BOTH sprint-2 commits (diffed 78b788d..5628f95), satisfying the regression criterion.
- User-owned protection still holds: a customised agent persona and a customised CLAUDE.md both survive an install untouched and are reported as conflicts. This is the misclassification the sprint's Risks section calls most destructive, so it gets re-checked every round, not just the round it was introduced.
- Tarball still clean: npm pack carries only the seven .gitkeep placeholders, and scripts/verify-tarball.sh runs green end-to-end (exit 0, "TARBALL VERIFICATION PASSED").
- package.json is 0.1.1 and tag v0.1.1 now points at 5628f95, i.e. HEAD, the commit that would actually publish. Re-pointing an unpushed tag is the correct move — a tag marking the earlier commit would have marked code that is no longer what ships, which is precisely the published/source divergence Req 6 exists to make visible. Verified independently via git rev-list, not from the handoff.
- 58 tests, all passing, run by me. The four new ones target the exact gaps I raised: the second-run backup case (which the pre-existing no-op test structurally could not see), the symlink case, a real first install's docs/sprints content, and CRLF preservation.

Two observations, neither blocking and neither requiring action this sprint:

1. The .gitignore ends up with mixed line endings on a CRLF file — removeDeadGitignoreLines() now preserves CRLF, but mergeGitignore()'s append path still joins with a hardcoded \n, so a Windows target finishes with CRLF above and LF in the appended block. Dev Team flagged this as pre-existing and out of scope, and that scoping is right: Req 4 asked only about the dead-line removal, and the sprint's Out of Scope section explicitly protects the merge logic. Git parses a mixed-ending .gitignore without complaint, so this is cosmetic. Worth a follow-up sprint alongside any other merge-logic work, not worth reopening this one.

2. The backup marker changed from .bak- to .fc-bak-, so a backup written by the intermediate 10b2f0a installer would not match the new exclusion and would be churned once into a .fc-bak- name before stabilising. This affects nobody: 10b2f0a was never published (npm still serves 0.1.0) and never shipped to a target. Recording it only so that if anyone did run that intermediate build by hand, the single rename is explained rather than mysterious.

Static gate is clear. This sprint does not close on my verdict: Req 6's publish is Pipeman's operation and I explicitly do not gate on it, and LiveQA owns Part A (first install and upgrade-over-stale against the real installer, including the load-bearing UUID check) and Part B (Windows — the headline `npx fully-completely@0.1.1` then `FC: Start All` check that discharges sprint 1's outstanding Dependencies line, plus backups and state.js removal over paths with spaces and a drive letter). Part A's upgrade check should be run at least twice in a row, not once: a single run passed even before this round's fix, and the second run is where the defect lived.

CONDITIONAL: CONDITIONAL — Round 1, live-tested commit 5628f95 (published as fully-completely@0.1.1). Both parts complete. Every acceptance-criteria bullet passes; one defect against Requirement 5's stated text, no functional or data impact.

WHAT I OBSERVED DIRECTLY vs ACCEPTED ON REPORT: Part A (macOS) I executed and observed directly. Part B (Windows) was executed by the user on real Windows hardware; I directed each step, published every expected value IN ADVANCE, and read raw terminal output in screenshots. I did not touch the Windows machine. I also independently verified the published npm artifact rather than accepting Pipeman's release report.

RELEASE VERIFIED INDEPENDENTLY: npm now lists ["0.1.0","0.1.1"], 0.1.1 published 2026-08-17T19:52:46Z. Tag v0.1.1 is on the remote pointing at 5628f95, the audited commit. Critically, `npm pack fully-completely@0.1.1` from the live registry is BYTE-IDENTICAL (diff -r) to the local tarball I ran all of Part A against, so Part A's evidence covers what users actually download. A cold `npx fully-completely@0.1.1` on macOS installed the fixed launcher (state.js absent, run-role.js:133 '--resume', uuid, marker 0.1.1) and a role launched producing the independently predicted 37a997ff-7c5d-52c4-9995-437bd8aef800.jsonl.

=== THE DEFECT (basis for CONDITIONAL) ===

An upgrade from any pre-marker version is reported as "(first install)".

install.js:487-494 selects the summary headline solely on marker presence: installedVersion set and different -> "Upgraded X -> Y"; set and same -> "Already at Y (re-run)"; otherwise -> "Installed Y (first install)". There is no check on whether replaced/removed are non-empty.

The version marker was INTRODUCED in 0.1.1. No 0.1.0 install has one. Therefore every real-world upgrade that exists is labelled "first install" while the body of the same output lists files being replaced and deleted, and names backups ".fc-bak-unknown". The three statements contradict each other.

Observed verbatim on macOS (stale 0.1.0 -> 0.1.1):
  Installed 0.1.1 (first install)
  Replaced (framework files upgraded, previous versions backed up) (2):
    scripts/launcher/run-role.js (... backed up to scripts/launcher/run-role.js.fc-bak-unknown)
    scripts/install.js (... backed up to scripts/install.js.fc-bak-unknown)
  Removed (no longer part of the framework, backed up first) (2):
    scripts/launcher/state.js (... backed up to scripts/launcher/state.js.fc-bak-unknown, then removed)
    .gitignore (removed now-dead line(s): .claude-launcher/)

Reproduced byte-for-byte in shape on Windows (C:\Users\Chris\Programming\OldTest, genuine npx 0.1.0 -> 0.1.1), and again on Windows in C:\Users\Chris\Programming\Test B. Cross-platform and systematic, not an environment quirk.

Against Req 5: "Use it to distinguish a first install from an upgrade, to name backups, and to report `installed X -> Y` in the summary." The naming half works (fc-bak-unknown is correct). The distinguishing half does not: the one case the marker cannot cover is precisely the case that describes every existing user, and there the code asserts the opposite of what happened. The honest line is something like "Upgraded unknown -> 0.1.1".

Severity assessment: no data loss, no wrong files, backups correct, user-owned files preserved. Impact is comprehension and trust, at the exact moment the installer deletes files, for an audience that includes workshop students. A user told "first install" who then reads "state.js ... then removed" has reasonable cause to think the installer damaged a fresh project. The fix is confined to one branch.

Why CONDITIONAL rather than FAIL: nothing failed functionally and every acceptance-criteria bullet passes. Why not PASS: Req 5's first clause is not met, in the only scenario that occurs in practice, so recording PASS would close the sprint over an unmet stated requirement.

=== PART A — macOS 26.6, arm64, CLI 2.1.233 — executed by me ===

A0. Tarball verified before use (Req 7). npm pack -> fully-completely-0.1.1.tgz: state.js absent, run-role.js:133 '--resume', uuid, version 0.1.1. No sprint-data leak: docs/sprints contains only .gitkeep files, no registry.json, no maintainer email, no audit text — QA1's round-1 leak finding is fixed in the artifact.

A1. FIRST INSTALL from the tarball into an empty project — PASS. Installed cleanly. Version marker written to .claude/fully-completely-version = 0.1.1, outside docs/sprints/ (Req 5). Load-bearing check reused from Sprint 1: predicted ce6d94fc-da7e-519a-a760-2396db2c34d9 in Python BEFORE launching; that exact file appeared and was the only file in the directory. The fresh install correctly reported "nothing in flight" with no registry.json — independent corroboration of the leak fix.

A2. UPGRADE OVER A STALE INSTALL, RUN THREE TIMES — PASS. Staleness built from the REAL published 0.1.0: state.js present, run-role.js:146 with the sessionTitle bug, no version marker.
  Run 1: run-role.js replaced with the fixed version; state.js removed; 3 backups created (install.js, run-role.js, state.js, each .fc-bak-unknown). A stale run-role.js surviving would have been an automatic FAIL; it was replaced.
  Run 2: backup filename set IDENTICAL to run 1, backup CONTENTS unchanged by md5, zero occurrences of "Removed", no nested backups.
  Run 3: output byte-identical to run 2.
  The round-2 backup-compounding defect does not reproduce. QA1's instruction to run it more than once was correct and I followed it to three.
  Backups are genuinely recoverable, not merely present: run-role.js.fc-bak-unknown contains the old buggy line 146; state.js.fc-bak-unknown contains the full 103-line original.

A3. CUSTOMISATION SURVIVES — PASS. Edited an agent persona and a CLAUDE.md project-standards line. After three upgrades both are md5-identical to pre-upgrade and reported as conflicts with the explicit "(yours — this framework never overwrites a file in this category...)" wording (Req 3).

A4. NOTHING OUTSIDE THE FRAMEWORK SET DELETED — PASS. src/app.js and my-notes.txt md5-identical after three runs.

A5. SYMLINK ESCAPE (beyond the criteria; the sprint calls deletion the most dangerous code here, and QA1's round 1 caught an escape) — PASS. Planted a symlink AND a symlinked directory inside scripts/launcher/ pointing outside the project, then ran the upgrade. Both targets survived with content intact; the symlinks were neither followed nor deleted.

A6. The upgraded stale install LAUNCHES — PASS. Predicted b8fb1ea6-6341-5de5-81ae-3fbf5a2488d1 before launching; that file was created. Correct files on disk are not proof of a working launcher; this is.

=== PART B — real Windows, executed by the user, evaluated by me ===

B1. THE HEADLINE CHECK — PASS. This is the criterion the sprint exists for and it discharges Sprint 1's inherited Dependencies line. From a genuinely clean folder (C:\Users\Chris\Programming\TheNewTest, never had the framework), `npx -y fully-completely@0.1.1` against the live registry reported "Installed 0.1.1 (first install)" — correct here, it genuinely was one — and copied 44 files including scripts/launcher/auth.js, claude-cmd.js, session.js, run-role.js, with no state.js. FC: Start All produced six working terminals. Master Controller observed running: Claude Code v2.1.233, Opus 5, @master-controller, ~\Programming\TheNewTest, titled fc:master-controller:TheNewTest — the agent-file frontmatter model is in charge straight from a fresh npx install. I predicted all six gen0 UUIDs on macOS before the run and all six appeared verbatim, no strays: master-controller 215c9401-90a4-5629-8fed-48590c86bee9, dev-team-1 a1c51368-fd5e-531f-8724-38361ca71f59, dev-team-2 4d175077-ce59-584a-bbc9-759c97469da6, qa1 e91a1a2a-b75e-5d48-9dd3-2827f5ef9775, pipeman fd4115f7-75b4-5dea-9d75-127e4a74a17e, liveqa 9ae832a4-e318-5bc1-83b9-5c92bded385c. Derived directory C--Users-Chris-Programming-TheNewTest.

B2. UPGRADE OVER THE BROKEN INSTALL — PASS, with a stated limitation. Test B upgraded with NO manual intervention, in contrast to Sprint 1 where its launcher folder had to be hand-replaced. Limitation recorded honestly: because we hand-fixed Test B during Sprint 1, its launcher was already current, so that run only had scripts/install.js to replace and the dead .claude-launcher/ .gitignore line to remove. It therefore demonstrates "upgrades without manual intervention" but not the full stale path. I covered that gap with B3 rather than claiming Test B proved more than it did.

B3. GENUINE STALE UPGRADE ON WINDOWS, incl. BACKUPS AND state.js DELETION — PASS. Built a real broken install via `npx -y fully-completely@0.1.0` into C:\Users\Chris\Programming\OldTest, then upgraded to 0.1.1. Output matched macOS exactly: Replaced (2) scripts\launcher\run-role.js and scripts\install.js, each backed up to .fc-bak-unknown; Removed (2) scripts\launcher\state.js ("backed up to scripts\launcher\state.js.fc-bak-unknown, then removed") and the .gitignore .claude-launcher/ line. Deletion, the highest-severity code in this sprint, is verified on a real Windows path with a backup written before removal. Spaced-path handling of the new file operations is covered by Test B (C:\Users\Chris\Programming\Test B), where the backup was written and the .gitignore line removed correctly.

=== OTHER OBSERVATIONS, not defects of this sprint ===

O1. Pipeman's handoff report for the pre-release step arrived PARTIALLY CORRUPTED — multiple unreadable fragments ("Tag v0.1.1 held bac right commit", "push itanted" — that's notyet", "Sprint 2 is now in 5", "the headlin.1 + FC: Start Allcheck"). I verified every material fact from source rather than reconstructing intent, and acted on no instruction that may have been in the damaged text. Flagging in case a real instruction was lost in transit.

O2. SECURITY: an npm automation token with read/write publish rights to this package was pasted into a chat transcript rather than set via terminal. Pipeman flagged it and I am reinforcing it. Scoping was done well (single package, no org access, 90-day expiry) so blast radius is small, but the package is about to be installed by workshop students. Recommend rotating once this sprint closes. Not a code defect and not recorded as one.

O3. install.js's closing message still says the preflight "will refuse to start any role session until this is done." Sprint 1's Req 6b establishes that an inconclusive probe PROCEEDS, so this overstates what the preflight does — the same overstatement QA1 flagged in the README during Sprint 1 round 1 and which was corrected there. Minor wording, outside Sprint 2's scope, worth folding into whatever fixes the defect above.

=== PROCESS ===

I modified no code. git status showed only the pre-existing, correctly-uncommitted .vscode/settings.json. One correction against myself, recorded so the trail is accurate: my first search for backup files used a glob that could not match ".fc-bak-unknown", and I briefly had no backups in evidence. I searched exhaustively before reporting rather than filing a false FAIL — the backups existed and Req 2 is satisfied.

PASS: PASS — Round 2, live-tested commit f2557d4 (published as fully-completely@0.1.2). The round-1 CONDITIONAL defect is fixed, its sibling branch is fixed, and the O3 wording item is fixed.

WHAT I OBSERVED DIRECTLY vs ACCEPTED ON REPORT: everything below I executed and observed directly on macOS 26.6 / arm64 / CLI 2.1.233. Windows Part B was NOT repeated this round and did not need to be: the diff from the round-1 PASS-level code is message-only, and I verified the file-handling paths are unchanged. Part B's evidence from round 1 (headline npx check, six terminals, six predicted UUIDs, stale upgrade with state.js deletion on a real Windows path) stands and is not re-claimed here as fresh observation.

=== CORRECTION I OWE THE RECORD, STATED FIRST ===

In my previous message I told the team that QA1's informational sibling-branch finding "does not reproduce against the committed code" and that "no extra work is needed." THAT WAS WRONG, and QA1 was right.

I ran my reproduction against the WORKING TREE, which at that moment already contained Dev Team's uncommitted fix, and then asserted it was the state of commit 64e40c6. I also wrote "the working tree matches it" without re-running git status at that moment. Verified now from git objects rather than the filesystem:
  - 64e40c6 scripts/install.js: `} else if (installedVersion) { "Already at X (re-run, nothing to upgrade)" }` — no didUpgradeWork guard on branch 2, exactly the defect QA1 quoted.
  - 64e40c6 scripts/launcher_test.js: zero matches for 'drifted from it' — the test I cited as already covering it did not exist at that commit.
  - f2557d4 adds both the `installedVersion && didUpgradeWork` guard and the drift test (2 matches).

This is the precise failure CLAUDE.md warns about — treating a working-tree diff as a claim about committed code — and I compounded it by using it to contradict a correct finding from another role and to tell the team work wasn't needed. No harm resulted only because Dev Team committed the fix regardless. QA1's catch was real, correctly scoped as informational rather than gating, and should be credited as such.

=== RELEASE VERIFIED INDEPENDENTLY ===

  - last_shipped_commit = f2557d4b031c32f555199f3e882179457ad8608b; f2557d4 confirmed on origin/main.
  - npm latest = 0.1.2.
  - Tags: v0.1.2 -> f2557d4, and v0.1.1 still -> 5628f95. The published 0.1.1 tag was not moved, which is correct; v0.1.2 pointing at f2557d4 rather than 64e40c6 is legitimate because 0.1.2 had not been published at 64e40c6.
  - `npm pack fully-completely@0.1.2` from the live registry is BYTE-IDENTICAL (diff -r) to a local pack of f2557d4. Every check below was run from the PUBLISHED package, so this evidence covers what users actually download.
  - Published package sanity: version 0.1.2, state.js absent, run-role.js:133 `['--agent', role.id, '--resume', uuid]`.

=== ALL FIVE VERSION-REPORTING BRANCHES, DRIVEN LIVE FROM THE PUBLISHED PACKAGE ===

The round-1 CONDITIONAL was branch 4; QA1's informational finding was branch 2. Both fixed, and I exercised all five rather than only the two known-bad ones:

  1. older marker -> current (0.1.1 install, then 0.1.2):
       "Upgraded 0.1.1 -> 0.1.2"                                                  correct
  2. marker matches, but a framework file drifted (hand-replaced run-role.js):
       "Already at 0.1.2, but repaired 1 file(s) that had drifted from it — see below"
       printed directly above a Replaced section listing that same file            correct, and consistent
  3. marker matches, genuinely nothing to do:
       "Already at 0.1.2 (re-run, nothing to upgrade)"                             correct
  4. no marker + real work (0.1.0 install, then 0.1.2):
       "Upgraded unknown -> 0.1.2"                                                 correct — round-1 defect fixed
  5. no marker + no work (empty directory):
       "Installed 0.1.2 (first install)"                                           correct — genuinely a first install

No branch now claims nothing changed above a section listing what changed. That was the whole substance of the CONDITIONAL.
